[MUJAHID:v1p69/r1] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | reports | He identifies the hypocrites' devils as their companions among the hypocrites and polytheists.
[MUQATIL:2:14-15/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The believers are the Prophet’s Companions who affirmed Muhammad; the hypocrites privately tell Jewish leaders Kaʿb b. al-Ashraf and his followers that they share their religion and feign faith only to mock Muhammad and his Companions.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p39#4/r1] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatada identifies the hypocrites’ ‘satans’ as the polytheists to whom they privately declare loyalty.
[IBNHISHAM:v1p531#2/r7] IBNHISHAM, d. 213 · author | holds | Their satans are Jews who urge the hypocrites to deny the truth and oppose what the Messenger brought.
[IBNHISHAM:v1p531#2/r8] IBNHISHAM, d. 213 · author | holds | Their assurance to their satans means that they share the same position as them.
[IBNHISHAM:v1p531#2/r9] IBNHISHAM, d. 213 · author | holds | They say they are only mocking and playing with the believers.
[IBNHISHAM:v2p547/r2] IBNHISHAM, d. 213 · ابن هشام | holds | A private confidant is someone secretly trusted apart from God; Ibn Hisham compares this concealed allegiance to hypocrites who publicly profess faith but privately tell their satans they are with them. | mentions 9:16
[AKHFASH:v1p50/r1] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | The plural wāw in لقوا is omitted when its sukūn meets the lām of الذين; the remaining form still signals plurality.
[AKHFASH:v1p50/r4] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | خلوت إلى فلان في حاجة can mean the same as خلوت بفلان, but the latter can also mean mocking him.
[AKHFASH:v1p50/r5] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | The preposition إلى can mean مع, as in من أنصاري إلى الله. | mentions 3:52
[AKHFASH:v1p50/r6] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | Prepositions can shift sense: من may mean على, باء may mean على, and في may mean على. | mentions 21:77, 3:75, 20:71
[AKHFASH:v1p50/r7] AKHFASH, d. 215 · يونس | reports | Yunus reports that Arabs use في أبيك for عليه, ظفرت عليه for به, and رضيت عليه for عنه.
[AKHFASH:v1p50/r8] AKHFASH, d. 215 · الشاعر | reports | An anonymous poetic example uses علي after رضيت to show the preposition's shifted sense.
[TAB-FULL:v1p306/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The hypocrites profess faith to believers to protect their lives, property, and families, then assure their leaders and fellow polytheists that they remain allies and only mock the believers.
[TAB-FULL:v1p306/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Jewish men told the Prophet’s companions they followed their religion, then told their own leaders they were with them and merely mocking.
[TAB-FULL:v1p306/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Their devils were Jews who urged them to deny the Messenger and oppose his teaching; they then claimed to share their companions’ religion.
[TAB-FULL:v1p308/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي | reports | The hypocrites’ devils are the leading figures in disbelief.
[TAB-FULL:v1p308/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Their devils are their chiefs and leaders in evil.
[TAB-FULL:v1p308/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | In another interpretation, their devils are the polytheists.
[TAB-FULL:v1p308/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Their devils are the hypocrites’ companions among the disbelievers.
[TAB-FULL:v1p308/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Their devils are their companions among hypocrites and polytheists.
[TAB-FULL:v1p308/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الربيع بن أنس | reports | Their devils are their brothers from among the polytheists.
[TAB-FULL:v1p308/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن جريج | reports | When believers prospered, hypocrites claimed fellowship with them, but in private they mocked the believers.
[TAB-FULL:v1p310/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | The phrase’s devils means the hypocrites’ companions among hypocrites and polytheists.
[TAB-FULL:v1p310/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · نحويي البصرة | reports | A Basran grammarian says khala ila means private conversation for a particular need, while khala bihi can mean either private need or mockery; ila avoids ambiguity.
[TAB-FULL:v1p310/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | An alternative analysis takes ila to mean with, since Arabic prepositions can substitute for one another; the cited verse uses ila in the sense of with. | mentions 3:52
[TAB-FULL:v1p310/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الشاعر | reports | The cited line uses ʿalayya to mean ʿannī, illustrating substitution among prepositions.
[TAB-FULL:v1p310/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · نحويي أهل الكوفة | prefers | The Kufan analysis takes the phrase as turning their private attention toward their devils; al-Tabari prefers it because ila has its own proper sense and should not be replaced without proof.
[TAB-FULL:v2p145/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The verse refers to Israelites who heard God’s word and distorted it after understanding; when they met believers they claimed to believe in Muhammad and his revelation, adopting hypocrites’ ways.
[TAB-FULL:v2p145/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Some Jews told Muhammad they believed, then privately asked one another whether to reveal what God had disclosed to them. | mentions 2:76
[TAB-FULL:v2p145/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الضحاك عن ابن عباس | reports | Jewish hypocrites said they believed when they met the Prophet’s companions.
[TAB-FULL:v2p145/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | They said they believed in the Prophet, but only for the believers’ benefit.
[TAB-FULL:v2p145/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي | reports | The people in question were Jews who believed and then became hypocrites.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p46/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Some Jews told the Prophet’s companions, when they met them, that they followed the companions’ religion.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p46/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | The Jews characterized Muhammad as the companions’ messenger, but said his message was specifically for them.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p46/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · أبو مالك | reports | The verb khala means that they went away.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p46/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Their devils were their brothers.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p46/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | The devils were Jewish leaders who urged them to deny and oppose what the Messenger brought.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p46/r6] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · قتادة | reports | Their devils were their leaders and chiefs in associating partners with God and in evil.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p46/r7] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مجاهد | reports | Their devils were their associates among the hypocrites and polytheists.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p46/r8] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · author | holds | The author identifies the devils as Jewish leaders, including Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, and notes that Abu al-ʿAliya, al-Suddi, and al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas explained it similarly.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p48/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | By saying they were with the hypocrites, they meant they followed the same religion as them.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p48/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Their claim that they were joking meant they were mocking Muhammad’s companions; Qatada and al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas report the same explanation. | mentions 2:15
[NAHHAS:v1p189/r10] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | In connected speech لقوا drops the vowel before wāw because it is already indicated; لاقوا keeps its vowel because the preceding letter is fatḥa.
[NAHHAS:v1p189/r11] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Alladhina is accusative as the object of آمنوا, which is inside its relative clause; قالوا آمنا answers إذا.
[NAHHAS:v1p189/r12] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | With a softened hamza in شياطينهم, its vowel transfers to wāw and the hamza is deleted, as in the Medinan reading.
[NAHHAS:v1p189/r13] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Shayatin is genitive after إلى; its broken plural keeps its nūn in construct, while the suffix is genitive by annexation.
[NAHHAS:v1p189/r14] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The underlying إنا is إننا, shortened to avoid successive nūns; معكم is accusative through an implied state of being.
[NAHHAS:v1p189/r15] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | reports | Those who give ʿayn sukun treat مع as a preposition.
[NAHHAS:v1p189/r16] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | إنما نحن مستهزءون is a nominal sentence; Sibawayh softens its hamza between hamza and wāw because its vowel belongs there.
[NAHHAS:v1p189/r17] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash instead makes the softened hamza a pure yāʾ, yielding مستهزيون, by analogy with his treatment of السفهاء. | mentions 2:13
[NAHHAS:v1p189/r18] NAHHAS, d. 338 · محمد بن يزيد | rejects | Ibn Yazid rejects al-Akhfash’s analogy: السفهاء requires wāw after softening toward alif, while مستهزئون has no such constraint. | mentions 2:13
[NAHHAS:v1p189/r19] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | A reader who replaces the hamza says مستهزون; this is the form written in the codex.
[NAHHAS:v1p189/r8] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The form لقيوا loses the yāʾ’s damma for heaviness, then drops the yāʾ where two sukūns meet.
[NAHHAS:v1p189/r9] NAHHAS, d. 338 · محمد بن السميفع اليماني | reports | Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa al-Yamani read لاقوا, whose underlying form is لاقيوا.
[THALABI:v1p154/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Here laqu means saw; its older form laqiyu was contracted because the kasra was heavy on ya and the adjacent waw and ya became sukuns.
[THALABI:v1p154/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس | reports | The verse was revealed about Abdullah ibn Ubayy: he professed support for Muhammad to Saʿd ibn ʿUbada, then urged his own leaders to cling to ancestral religion.
[THALABI:v1p154/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس | reports | Abdullah ibn Ubayy publicly praised Abu Bakr, Umar, and Ali, but after Ali rebuked his hypocrisy he told companions to imitate his double dealing; Muslims reported it to the Prophet and the verse came down.
[THALABI:v1p155/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · محمد بن السميقع |

 reports | He reads laqu as laqu, with the same meaning.
[THALABI:v1p155/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Their assurance إنا معكم means they remain on the leaders' religion and are their supporters; they mock Muhammad and his companions.
[THALABI:v1p155/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The believers whom the hypocrites meet are Abu Bakr and his companions, to whom they say they believe as they do.
[THALABI:v1p155/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Khala means they returned; khala bihi, ilayhi, and maʿahu all mean being alone with someone.
[THALABI:v1p155/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · النضر بن شميل | reports | In this construction ila can mean maʿa, as in Qur'anic expressions and two poetic examples. | mentions 2:187, 4:2, 3:52
[THALABI:v1p155/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Their shayatin are their leaders, chiefs, guides, and soothsayers.
[THALABI:v1p155/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس | reports | He identifies five Jewish leaders as their devils: Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf in Medina, Abu Burda among Aslam, Abdullah in Juhayna, Awf ibn Amir among Asad, and Abdullah ibn al-Sawda in Syria.
[THALABI:v1p155/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Shaytan is any rebellious disobedient being, human or jinn; the term also applies to snakes and troublesome animals. | mentions 37:65
[THALABI:v1p155/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | A prophetic report calls a rider who crosses before a praying person, then refuses to stop, a devil; another calls a man following a flying pigeon a devil following a devil, meaning a wicked pursuer.
[THALABI:v1p155/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو النجم | reports | His verse jokes that every human poet has a female devil while his own devil is male.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p76/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن عباس | reports | Their devils are Jews who urge them to disbelieve.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p76/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن مسعود | reports | Their devils are the leaders among them in unbelief.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p76/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | One reading takes إلى as مع, meaning they are with their devils, as in the cited verse. | mentions 3:52
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p76/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · بعض البصريين | reports | To be alone with someone toward a need can be expressed as خلوْت إلى; خلوْت به can also mean mockery, making this wording more eloquent and literal.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p76/r5] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · بعض الكوفيين | reports | The phrase means that the hypocrites returned to their devils.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p76/r6] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Shayṭān may derive from shatana, to be far away: either far from good or far in its evil path; on this derivation the ن is root-letter.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p76/r7] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Another derivation connects shayṭān to shāṭa, to perish; the cited line uses يشيط for perishing, and ن is then an added letter.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p76/r8] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | prefers | The decisive derivation makes shayṭān a faʿlān from burning, naming it for its eventual state.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p76/r9] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Their claim of being with the believers means they share the leaders' disbelief and hostility; calling themselves mockers means their displayed assent is feigned.
[WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p21/r6] WAHIDI-ASBAB, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says the verse concerns Abdullah b. Ubayy and his companions: he warmly praised Abu Bakr, Umar, and Ali before believers, then told his followers to imitate him and mock them; the Muslims reported this to the Prophet, and the verse was revealed.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p164#2/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · المفسرون | reports | The believers whom the hypocrites meet are identified as Abū Bakr and his companions.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p164#2/r10] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو علي | holds | Abū ʿAlī argues shayṭān is fayʿāl from shatana, not faʿlān from yashīṭ; the following segment gives his morphological evidence.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p164#2/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The form laqū comes from laqiyū; a heavy yāʾ was dropped and its ḍamma transferred to the preceding qāf.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p164#2/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الحراني عن ابن السكيت | reports | Ibn al-Sikkīt lists the forms liqāʾ, liqyān, liqyā, and laqā for meeting.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p164#2/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الليث | reports | Al-Layth says a thing is met when it faces or encounters another thing.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p164#2/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · النضر | reports | Al-Nadr takes ilā in khalaw ilā as maʿa and cites parallels in 2:187, 3:52 and 61:14, and 4:2. | mentions 2:187, 3:52, 61:14, 4:2
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p164#2/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | prefers | The grammarians understand the hypocrites as leaving believers and going to their chiefs; the author prefers the ordinary endpoint sense of ilā over treating it as maʿa.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p164#2/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | A shayṭān is any rebellious, defiant being among jinn or humans, as 6:112 calls human and jinn tempters shayāṭīn. | mentions 6:112
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p164#2/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الليث | reports | Al-Layth derives shayṭān as fayʿāl from shatana, to be distant; he also connects shayṭana with becoming and acting like Satan.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p164#2/r9] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · قوم | reports | Some derive shayṭān as faʿlān from shāṭa, to perish or burn; al-Aʿshā’s verse yushīṭ is cited as evidence.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p169/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو علي | holds | Abū ʿAlī rejects faʿlān because Sibawayh attests shayṭana on the fayʿal pattern; Amiyya’s shāṭin likewise has n as the root’s final radical, establishing shayṭān as fayʿāl.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p169/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو علي | holds | Amiyya’s line is decisive: shāṭin is an active participle with n as its final root consonant, so shayṭān is fayʿāl and not faʿlān from yashīṭ.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p169/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abū Isḥāq explains shayṭān as one extreme in unbelief and far removed from the truth, among jinn or humans.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p169/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says the hypocrites’ shayāṭīn are their chiefs and leaders.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p169/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Maʿa joins one thing to another and is accusative like an adverb because ana maʿaka means I am settled with you.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p169/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Huzʾ means ridicule: the mocker outwardly shows something other than what is inward, to belittle and play around.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:13-16/r2] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | When alone with their leaders, they profess loyalty to their religion and say their public profession is mockery, displaying what they do not inwardly believe.
[DAMGHANI:v1p263/r4] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | The hypocrites’ shayāṭīn are their soothsayers, including Kaʿb b. al-Ashraf and others.
[DAMGHANI:v1p436/r6] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | In 2:14, maʿakum means that the hypocrites share their leaders’ religion; the same use appears of those with Hud and of the speaker’s companions. | mentions 11:58, 67:28
[JISHUMI:v1p255/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The transmitted reading is لقوا; a variant لاقوا has the same sense, but recitation must follow what is widely transmitted from the Prophet and Companions.
[JISHUMI:v1p255/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الخليل | reports | Meeting is the opposite of being screened; fundamentally it is two things encountering one another face to face.
[JISHUMI:v1p255/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | خلا is the opposite of being among others; mockery and derision are synonyms of jest, while seriousness is their opposite.
[JISHUMI:v1p255/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو عبيدة | reports | He defines Satan as any rebellious being among jinn, humans, or animals; another lexicographer defines one as rebellious from any species.
[JISHUMI:v1p255/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Two etymologies are offered: Satan may be distant from good (form fayʿāl) or associated with burning (form faʿlān); the verb means becoming satan-like.
[JISHUMI:v1p255/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | لقوا derives from لقيوا, with the vowel moved and adjacent silent letters resolved by deleting the wāw.
[JISHUMI:v1p255/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | إلى may mean ‘with,’ as in 3:52 and an Arabic proverb, or mark a destination; here it marks turning from believers to leaders. | mentions 3:52
[JISHUMI:v1p255/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | خلوت به can mean mocking someone or being alone with him, whereas خلوت إليه indicates making him the destination of one's need.
[JISHUMI:v1p255/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | إنا contracts إننا by deleting the second nūn to avoid a doubled consonant; the full form also occurs in Qur'anic usage.
[JISHUMI:v1p257/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | After the hypocrites said they would remain well as long as the other party lived, the Muslims reported what happened to the Messenger, and God revealed this verse.
[JISHUMI:v1p257/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The hypocrites professed belief in what was revealed to Muhammad when they met believers in order to protect their lives and property.
[JISHUMI:v1p257/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن عباس | prefers | ‘Their satans’ means their leaders among disbelievers; al-Jishumī prefers this over jinn because most scholars hold it, it is more natural, and the context excludes soothsayers. Al-Kalbi reports jinn satans.
[JISHUMI:v1p257/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن عباس | reports | Another report identifies their leaders as five Jews, including Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and Abu Burda.
[JISHUMI:v1p257/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | ‘We are with you’ means either that they share their leaders' religion or that they are their supporters.
